lines.text: Before the cup. Before the café. There was a forest, a red berry, and a story that would circle the earth.
High in the Ethiopian highlands, in cool mountain air, the coffee tree first took root — wild and forgotten.
Coffea arabica. A single delicate species that today fills more cups than any other.
Legend tells of Kaldi, a young herder, who watched his goats dance through the night after eating a bright red cherry. Curious, he tasted it too.
Carried across the Red Sea to Yemen, the roasted bean found its name — qahwa. Sufi mystics drank it to stay awake through nights of prayer. From the port of Mocha, it sailed to the world.
Months later, the cherries ripen to deep crimson — and only the reddest are ready to be picked.
The finest coffee is still gathered the oldest way — by hand, one ripe cherry at a time.
A single tree gives only about a pound of roasted coffee a year.
Spread on raised beds, the cherries dry for weeks under the sun, turned again and again.
Inside every cherry, a pale green seed — the bean, still holding all its flavour in silence.
Then, fire. In the roaster's drum, heat begins to wake the sleeping bean.
It swells, browns, and near two hundred degrees — cracks open, releasing the aroma we know as coffee.
Seconds decide everything. The roaster reads colour and scent, and pulls the beans at the perfect moment.
Ground too soon, the aroma fades — so it waits until the last moment.
The first splash of water, and the grounds bloom — releasing gas, and proof the coffee is fresh.
In Ethiopia, where it all began, coffee returns home — poured from the clay jebena in a ceremony centuries old.
Elsewhere, the same patience — water circling slowly, drawing the flavour out in a spiral.
And at last, the cup — the whole long journey, held in your hands.
For six hundred years, coffee has done one quiet thing best — it brings people to the same table.
A warmth in the palms on a cold morning — small, and somehow enough.
From a wild forest berry to the cup in your hand — every step, remembered in the taste.
And behind every good cup, a pair of hands — and a craft, passed on with care.
From the highlands of Ethiopia to your morning cup — this is the soul of coffee. Thank you for watching History Frames Film.
